456.title: Discernment is the way (2.26–2.28)
456.hook: the cure is to tell the seer from the seen, not once in a flash but steadily, and the limbs of yoga make the light grow
456.howItsDone: In the Yoga tradition, discernment between awareness and what it is aware of is the central means of liberation, cultivated over years through study, the ethical disciplines and meditation, usually under a teacher's guidance.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the purpose of the world, and your line, for the seer. Experience and liberation, both. Did one ordinary thing get fully tasted, then let go? Day four hundred fifty-six.

Identical twins walk into a room. Strangers mix them up all evening. Their teacher gets it right most days. Their mother never gets it wrong, not even from behind, not even half asleep. She didn't learn that in one moment of insight. She learned it in ten thousand ordinary mornings, until telling them apart stopped being an effort and became the way she sees. Patanjali has named the disease and its cause. Today he names the cure and the remedy, and the remedy works a lot like that mother's eyes.
screen: `IDENTICAL TWINS.` → `STRANGERS MIX THEM UP.` → `THEIR MOTHER NEVER DOES.`

segments.voice: First the cure. Sutras 2.23 to 2.25 trace the knot: the seer and the seen are joined because of avidya, not seeing clearly. Take away the not-seeing, and the joining falls apart. Patanjali calls that removal the seer's aloneness. Freedom. Then sutra 2.26 gives the remedy. Viveka-khyati, aviplava. Viveka means discernment, telling one thing from another, the way you'd sift grain from husk. Khyati is the clear seeing of it. And aviplava is the word to circle: unwavering. Not a flash on a mountaintop that's gone by Monday. Steady. The mother's eyes, not the stranger's lucky guess. Sutra 2.27 says that for the one with this steady discernment, wisdom arrives in seven stages, all the way to the end. The sutra doesn't list them. The classical commentary does. Then 2.28 sets up the rest of the book. By practicing the limbs of yoga, impurity dwindles, and the light of knowledge shines brighter, all the way to discernment. Think of a lamp with a sooty glass. You don't make more light. You keep wiping the glass. So the long list that starts tomorrow, the eight limbs, isn't a set of rules for their own sake. It's how the glass gets wiped. On an ordinary Tuesday, viveka is tiny and practical: this is a thought, not a fact. This is my mood, not who I am. Said once, it's a flash. Said every day, it becomes how you see.
screen: `THE CURE: NO MORE NOT-SEEING.` · `VIVEKA — TELLING APART.` · `AVIPLAVA — UNWAVERING.` · `THE LIMBS WIPE THE SOOTY GLASS.` · then, large: `VIVEKA.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is small sorting, done steadily. Sit and let the breath settle. When a thought arrives, a plan, a worry, a song, quietly note: seen. When a feeling arrives: seen. When the body speaks up: seen. No need to push anything away. Just keep telling the watched from the watching, the way the mother tells the twins apart. If you lose the thread, that's fine. Pick it up again. The steadiness is in coming back. The bell holds the time.
Discernment is the way. Viveka, telling the seer from the seen, held steady enough that it stops wavering.
Your line: viveka. Today, when a hard thought shows up, try one quiet sentence: this is a thought, not a fact. Say it again the next time too. Day four hundred fifty-six.

457.title: The eight limbs (2.29)
457.hook: one sutra lists eight limbs of yoga, from how you treat others to absorption, and only one of them is a posture
457.tomorrow: Yama — non-harm, truth, non-stealing, restraint, non-grasping
457.howItsDone: Many teachers of yoga, in India and around the world, present the eight limbs of 2.29 as the framework of the whole practice, starting with the ethical restraints and observances, with posture and breath as preparation for meditation.

segments.voice: Yesterday: discernment is the way. Viveka, telling the seer from the seen, held steady. Did you try this is a thought, not a fact? Day four hundred fifty-seven.

Look at the timetable on the wall of almost any yoga studio, from Delhi to Minneapolis. Somewhere on it: Ashtanga, six p.m. Bring water. Expect to sweat. That class is a real modern tradition, built in the twentieth century in Mysore. But the word on the timetable is far older than the class. It comes from a single sutra, 2.29, a list of eight words. And if you read the list, you'll notice something that might surprise the six p.m. crowd. Of the eight, exactly one is a posture.
screen: `ASHTANGA, SIX P.M.` → `BRING WATER.` → `A LIST OF EIGHT WORDS.`

segments.voice: Ashta means eight. Anga means limb, a part of a body. Yesterday Patanjali said that by practicing the limbs of yoga, impurity dwindles and discernment shines. Today he lists them. Yama, the restraints: how you treat others. Niyama, the observances: how you treat yourself. Asana, the seat. Pranayama, working with the breath. Pratyahara, the senses drawing back. Dharana, concentration. Dhyana, meditation. And samadhi, absorption. Listen to the direction of that list. It starts outside, with other people, and moves steadily inward: your habits, your body, your breath, your senses, your attention, until there's only the object shining. Later, at the start of book three, Patanjali calls the last three inner limbs, more internal than the first five. Teachers read the shape in different ways. Some hear a ladder: get the ethics right, then the body, then the mind. Others lean on the word itself. Limbs, not rungs. A child's arms and legs don't grow one after another. They grow together. Both readings have long histories, and the sutra doesn't settle it. What the sutra does settle is the proportion. Ethics first, twice. Posture, one word out of eight. Meditation and absorption at the end, where the whole thing is heading. Over the next days we'll take the limbs one by one. Today, just hold the whole body of it.
screen: `ASHTA: EIGHT. ANGA: LIMB.` · `FROM OTHERS, INWARD TO ABSORPTION.` · `A LADDER, OR LIMBS GROWING TOGETHER?` · `ONE POSTURE OUT OF EIGHT.` · then, large: `ASHTANGA.`

segments.voice: Today's practice walks all eight limbs in miniature. Hold a moment of goodwill toward someone, that's the first limb. Settle into feeling content with this exact moment, the second. Let your seat be steady and easy, the third. Let the breath lengthen a little, the fourth. Let sounds and sights stay in the background, the fifth. Rest your attention on one point, maybe the breath at the nostrils, the sixth. Let that attention flow without breaks, the seventh. And if it happens, let the point fill everything, the eighth. If it doesn't, that's normal. The bell holds the time.
The eight limbs. Ashtanga, the eight parts of yoga in sutra 2.29, from how you treat others all the way in to absorption.
Your line: ashtanga. Today, count the eight on your fingers once, yama to samadhi, and notice which limb you've practiced least this week. Day four hundred fifty-seven.

458.title: Yama — non-harm, truth, non-stealing, restraint, non-grasping (2.30–2.31)
458.hook: the first limb of yoga is five restraints, and the commentary says every one of them grows from the first, non-harm
458.tomorrow: Niyama — cleanliness, contentment, discipline, study, surrender
458.howItsDone: In many Hindu yoga lineages, the five yamas are taught before any posture or breathing practice, and renunciants may take them as formal vows, while householders often practice them as everyday ethics.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the eight limbs, ashtanga, from how you treat others all the way in to absorption. Which limb did you find you'd practiced least? Today, the first one. Day four hundred fifty-eight.

If you were writing a manual for reaching the deepest stillness a human mind can know, what would you put on page one? A breathing method, maybe. A secret posture. A mantra. Patanjali's page one has none of those. It says: don't hurt anyone. Don't lie. Don't take what isn't yours. Rein yourself in. Don't hoard. It reads less like a mystic's manual and more like a list a grandmother pins to the fridge. And that's exactly the point. He's telling you the stillness starts in the kitchen, with how you speak to the people in it.
screen: `PAGE ONE OF THE MANUAL.` → `NOT A TECHNIQUE.` → `A LIST FOR THE FRIDGE.`

segments.voice: Sutra 2.30 names the five yamas, the restraints. Ahimsa, non-harm. Satya, truthfulness. Asteya, not stealing. Brahmacharya, restraint, which the classical commentary reads as sexual restraint and celibacy for the renunciant; many householder teachers today read it as faithfulness and moderation. And aparigraha, not grasping, not piling up more than you need. Now the key move, from the classical commentary traditionally credited to Vyasa. Ahimsa comes first because it's the root. The other four, it says, are there for its sake, to make non-harm purer. So truth is in service of non-harm. The commentary is blunt about it: speech should be for the good of all beings, and a true sentence spoken to wound only looks like virtue. Ahimsa first. Then sutra 2.31 raises the stakes. These five become the great vow, mahavrata, when they apply everywhere, with no exceptions for kind of being, place, time or occasion. The commentary gives a fisherman as the example of a limited vow: I'll harm only fish. Or: not at the holy place. Not on the holy day. A limited vow is still a vow. But the great vow has no fine print. This word ahimsa has traveled far. Jains and Buddhists have long held it at the center of their own paths, and in the twentieth century Gandhi carried it into politics. In the sutras, though, it's quieter. It's page one.
screen: `FIVE RESTRAINTS.` · `AHIMSA IS THE ROOT.` · `TRUTH THAT WOUNDS ONLY LOOKS LIKE VIRTUE.` · `THE GREAT VOW HAS NO FINE PRINT.` · then, large: `AHIMSA FIRST.`

segments.voice: Today's practice tries non-harm on the inside first. Sit and let the breath settle. Notice the tone of the voice in your head. When a thought shows up, notice whether it arrives with a little harshness, toward yourself or someone else. You don't need to argue with it. Just soften the tone, the way you'd lower your voice near a sleeping child, and let the thought go on its way. Then rest with the breath until the next one. The bell holds the time.
Yama. The restraints, the first limb of yoga: non-harm, truth, non-stealing, restraint and non-grasping.
Your line: ahimsa first. Today, before one true thing you need to say, check it once against non-harm, and find a way to say it that doesn't wound. Day four hundred fifty-eight.

459.title: Niyama — cleanliness, contentment, discipline, study, surrender (2.32)
459.hook: the second limb turns from others to yourself, and three of its five are old friends from the start of book two
459.tomorrow: In the presence of one grounded in non-harm, hostility ceases
459.howItsDone: In many Hindu homes and yoga lineages, the niyamas shape daily life: bathing before worship, fasting or other disciplines, reading scripture or repeating a mantra, and offering one's actions to God.

segments.voice: Yesterday: yama, the five restraints, and your line, ahimsa first. Did one true thing get said without the wound? Day four hundred fifty-nine.

Twelve days ago, at the very start of book two, Patanjali gave a three-part practice for people who weren't born calm. He called it kriya yoga: discipline, study, surrender. Then he went off to diagnose the afflictions, the karma, the suffering, the cause. Now he's listing the second limb of yoga, five observances. And read them: cleanliness, contentment, and then, discipline, study, surrender. The same three words, back again, waiting in the second limb like friends at the end of a long hallway. He never forgot them. He was building the house around them.
screen: `KRIYA YOGA, TWELVE DAYS AGO.` → `DISCIPLINE, STUDY, SURRENDER.` → `BACK AGAIN IN THE SECOND LIMB.`

segments.voice: Sutra 2.32 names the niyamas, the observances. If the yamas are about how you treat others, these are about how you keep yourself. Shaucha, cleanliness. The classical commentary means two kinds: the outer kind, water and clean food, and the inner kind, washing away the mind's stains. Santosha, contentment, not wanting more than what you have at hand. Tapas, discipline. The word means heat, and the commentary describes it as bearing the pairs: hunger and thirst, cold and heat, standing and sitting. Svadhyaya, study, which the commentary explains as reading the texts on freedom, or repeating Om. And ishvara-pranidhana, surrender to Ishvara, the Lord, offering every action to the highest teacher. Five on the outside of you, five on the inside. The yamas, then the second five. Right after the list, Patanjali adds a tool for when it all goes wrong, and it may be the most practical sentence in the book. When contrary thoughts disturb you, he says in 2.33, cultivate the opposite. The commentary imagines someone tempted to lie, or to hurt, and has them say to themselves: I'm burning in the fires of the world, and now I'd go back to the very things I gave up, like a dog eating what it threw up. Not pretty. But memorable. You don't defeat the harsh thought by force. You put its opposite next to it, on purpose, and let that one grow.
screen: `THE SECOND FIVE: HOW YOU KEEP YOURSELF.` · `CLEAN, CONTENT, DISCIPLINED.` · `STUDY, AND SURRENDER TO ISHVARA.` · `WHEN IT GOES WRONG: THE OPPOSITE.` · then, large: `THE SECOND FIVE.`

segments.voice: Today's practice touches each of the second five, lightly. Sit and notice one clean thing, the breath moving in and out, a washed feeling. Then contentment: this seat, this moment, nothing to add. Then a little heat: stay still through one small itch without scratching. Then study: watch your own mind for a few breaths, as if reading it. Then, if you pray, you can offer the rest of the sit to God, or simply let go of trying. The bell holds the time.
Niyama. The observances, the second limb of yoga: cleanliness, contentment, discipline, study and surrender to Ishvara.
Your line: the second five. Today, when a harsh thought shows up, try 2.33: set its opposite right beside it, on purpose, and see which one grows. Day four hundred fifty-nine.

460.title: In the presence of one grounded in non-harm, hostility ceases (2.35–2.39)
460.word: In the presence of one grounded
460.hook: each restraint, once it's truly rooted, bears fruit, and the first fruit is that hostility drops away around you
460.howItsDone: Hindu stories of sages often describe their hermitages as places where wild animals live at peace, and teachers of the Yoga Sutras present the fruits of 2.35–2.39 as signs that the restraints have taken root, whether read as powers or as the natural results of an ethical life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: niyama, the second five, how you keep yourself. Did you set an opposite beside a harsh thought, and see which one grew? Day four hundred sixty.

A family dinner is going badly. Two cousins are one comment away from a real fight. Then a grandmother comes in from the kitchen, sits down, asks someone about their garden, and somehow, the air changes. Nobody decided to calm down. Nobody was told off. The fight just lost its footing. Most people have met someone like that, maybe once. Patanjali has met them too. Having listed the five restraints, he now says what happens when each one is truly rooted in a person. And the first fruit he names is that grandmother.
screen: `A DINNER ABOUT TO GO WRONG.` → `SOMEONE SITS DOWN.` → `THE AIR CHANGES.`

segments.voice: Sutra 2.35: when someone is grounded in non-harm, hostility is given up in their presence. Not their hostility. Everyone else's. The word for grounded means firmly established, standing on it. The classical commentary says that around such a person all creatures abandon their enmity, and later tellings picture hermitages where tigers and deer rest side by side. Then the fruits of the other four. Sutra 2.36: for one grounded in truth, actions and their results rest on their word. The commentary says if such a person says, be good, the listener becomes good, because their words don't fail. Sutra 2.37: for one grounded in not stealing, all jewels come near. Sutra 2.38: for one grounded in restraint, vigor is gained. Sutra 2.39: for one grounded in not grasping, there's insight into the how and why of one's births. How should these be read? Within the tradition, many have taken them as real powers that come with mastery. Others read them as the natural shape of a life. People drop their guard around someone who will never hurt them. Words carry weight when they never lie. The one who never takes is the one trusted with the treasure. The sutra doesn't choose for you. But notice one thing both readings share. The fruit doesn't come from trying to get the fruit. It comes from being grounded, standing on the restraint so long it's no longer an effort. The grandmother at the table isn't performing calm. She just stopped carrying a weapon years ago.
screen: `AROUND NON-HARM, HOSTILITY DROPS.` · `TRUTH: WORDS THAT DON'T FAIL.` · `JEWELS, VIGOR, INSIGHT INTO BIRTHS.` · `POWERS, OR THE SHAPE OF A LIFE?` · then, large: `THE FRUITS OF THE YAMAS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice notices what you bring into a room. Sit and let the breath settle. Picture walking into the next room you'll enter today, maybe a kitchen, an office, a group chat. Notice whether you're carrying anything sharp: a grievance, a comeback, a scorecard. You don't have to drop it by force. Just set it down for the length of this sit, the way you'd leave a heavy bag by the door, and breathe as someone with nothing to defend. The bell holds the time.
In the presence of one grounded in non-harm, hostility ceases. The first of five fruits that come when the restraints are fully rooted.

461.title: Contentment brings unsurpassed happiness (2.40–2.45)
461.hook: the fruits of the five observances, and the one Patanjali calls happiness with nothing above it
461.howItsDone: Teachers of the Yoga Sutras often single out santosha as a daily practice of accepting what is at hand, and many Hindus link it to gratitude in worship, offering food to God before eating and receiving it back as a blessing.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the fruits of the yamas. Around one grounded in non-harm, hostility drops away. Did you walk into a tense moment carrying nothing sharp? Day four hundred sixty-one.

A seven-year-old's birthday. For weeks there has been one gift on the list, the only thing that matters. Morning comes, the paper tears, and there it is. Pure joy. By lunchtime it's on the floor and the question has started: what can I ask for next? Nobody's a bad kid here. It's just how wanting works, at seven and at seventy. The new phone, the promotion, the house with one more room. Yesterday Patanjali gave the fruits of the five restraints. Today, the fruits of the five observances. And one of them, he says, beats every gift on every list.
screen: `ONE GIFT ON THE LIST.` → `BY LUNCH: WHAT NEXT?` → `THE FRUITS OF THE OBSERVANCES.`

segments.voice: The fruits come quickly in sutras 2.40 to 2.45. From cleanliness, a certain distance from your own body, then a clear, cheerful, one-pointed mind. From discipline, the body and senses perfected as impurity burns off. From study, meeting your chosen deity. From surrender to Ishvara, the perfection of samadhi itself. But in the middle sits one line that's simpler than all the rest. Sutra 2.42: from contentment, unsurpassed happiness. Santosha. Anuttama, the word for unsurpassed, means nothing higher, nothing above it. Not the best happiness so far. The top. The classical commentary backs it up with an old verse. Whatever pleasure desire brings in this world, and whatever great pleasure there is in heaven, together they aren't worth a sixteenth part of the happiness that comes when craving ends. A sixteenth. Notice what contentment is not, in this teaching. It isn't settling. It isn't pretending you don't want anything, or that a hard situation is fine. The commentary describes it as not wanting more than what's already at hand. Ambition can stay. The ache that follows every gift is what goes. The birthday child doesn't need a better gift. The gift was never the problem. The asking for the next one was. And here's the part worth repeating tonight: Patanjali places the highest happiness not at the end of getting, but at the end of wanting. It doesn't arrive. It's what's left.
screen: `THE FRUITS OF THE OBSERVANCES.` · `FROM CONTENTMENT: NOTHING HIGHER.` · `NOT WORTH A SIXTEENTH PART.` · `NOT SETTLING. THE END OF WANTING.` · then, large: `SANTOSHA.`

segments.voice: Today's practice looks for enough. Sit and let the breath settle. Notice one thing that's already here and already enough: the breath arriving without being asked, the chair holding you up, a little warmth in your hands. Stay with it. When the mind starts listing what's missing, the email, the plan, the thing you want next, notice the list, and come back to the one thing that's enough. You don't have to feel blissful. Just let enough be enough for two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Contentment brings unsurpassed happiness. Sutra 2.42: from santosha, a happiness with nothing above it.
Your line: santosha. Today, the next time you catch yourself thinking I'll be happy when, finish the sentence with right now, and see if it's true. Day four hundred sixty-one.

462.title: Asana — steady and comfortable (2.46–2.48)
462.hook: the most famous part of yoga gets three short sutras, and the first one is just three words: a seat, steady and comfortable
462.howItsDone: In the Yoga Sutras, asana is the seated posture for meditation, steady and easy; many Hindus who meditate or do japa sit cross-legged on a mat or cushion, while modern posture classes draw on later hatha yoga traditions.

segments.voice: Yesterday: contentment brings unsurpassed happiness. Santosha, the happiness at the end of wanting. Did 'I'll be happy when' turn into 'right now,' even once? Day four hundred sixty-two, the end of a week.

Search the word yoga on any phone and count the bodies. Legs behind heads. Handstands on paddleboards. Whole books of poses, hundreds of them, with names like crow and pigeon and downward dog. Now open the Yoga Sutras, the classic text so many of those books thank in their introductions, and look for the poses. You'll find the third limb, asana, in sutra 2.46. It's three words long in Sanskrit. Then two more short sutras. Then Patanjali moves on to the breath. That's the whole section.
screen: `HUNDREDS OF POSES ONLINE.` → `OPEN THE YOGA SUTRAS.` → `THREE SHORT SUTRAS.`

segments.voice: Sutra 2.46: sthira sukham asanam. Sthira, steady. Sukha, easy, comfortable. Asana, seat. The word comes from a root meaning to sit. It's the seat you meditate in. Steady and comfortable, both at once. Not rigid. Not slumped. Sutra 2.47 says how: by relaxing effort, and letting the mind rest in the endless. Some commentators hear in that word Ananta, the great serpent who holds up the earth without strain. Sutra 2.48 gives the result: then you're not knocked about by the pairs, heat and cold, comfort and discomfort. That's all it says. The classical commentary adds a few names of seats, the lotus, the hero's seat and others, but no instructions, no sequence. The long lists of postures came later, in hatha yoga texts many centuries after, and many historians argue that much of today's posture practice took its present shape in the last hundred years or so. None of that makes the postures wrong. It just tells you what Patanjali was after: a body quiet enough to forget, so the inner limbs can begin. Now look back over the week. Discernment is the way, steady seeing. The eight limbs, from others inward. Yama, ahimsa first. Niyama, the second five. Grounded in non-harm, hostility ceases. Contentment, nothing higher. And today, a seat. A week of the outer limbs, and almost none of it was about the body. Most of it was about how you treat people, including yourself.
screen: `STHIRA, SUKHA: STEADY, EASY.` · `RELAX THE EFFORT.` · `NO LONGER KNOCKED BY THE PAIRS.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `THAT'S ALL IT SAYS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is the whole of 2.46. Find a seat, chair, cushion or floor. First, steady: let the spine rise a little, the base settle down. Then easy: drop the shoulders, unclench the jaw, soften the hands. If something strains, adjust it. Then relax the effort of holding the pose at all, and let the body be held by whatever's under it. When an itch or ache asks for attention, notice it like weather. Steady. Easy. The bell holds the time.
Asana. The seat, the third limb of yoga, which Patanjali describes in three words: steady and comfortable.
Your line: that's all it says. Today, wherever you sit, a desk, a bus, a waiting room, check once: steady? easy? Adjust until both are true. Day four hundred sixty-two.

screen: `DAY 462 COUNTS.` → `A WEEK OF THE OUTER LIMBS, DONE.` → `TOMORROW: PRANAYAMA.`
